summary: Defines the SIP P-Served-User private header for the 3GPP IP Multimedia Subsystem. It solves a problem between the S-CSCF and an application server on the ISC interface by identifying which user a request is being handled for.

plainLanguage.summary: P-Served-User is a SIP header for trusted nodes in an IP Multimedia Subsystem. It tells an application server which user's service profile applies, even if forwarding changes other address fields. The header must stay inside its trust domain.

subtitle: A private SIP header identifies the user whose profile an IMS service is handling.

tldr.problem: In 3GPP IMS, an application server may infer the served user from a Request-URI or P-Asserted-Identity field. Forwarding can change those fields, making that inference wrong.
tldr.mechanism: P-Served-User carries the served user's identity and optional session-case and registration-state parameters. Proxies insert and use the header only within a configured trust domain, and remove it before forwarding outside that domain.
tldr.outcome: The header provides an explicit identity for trusted IMS nodes, but the RFC says it is generally unsuitable for inter-domain or Internet-wide use. RFC 5502 is Informational and has been updated by RFCs 8217 and 8498.

today: RFC 5502 is Informational and has been updated by RFC 8217 and RFC 8498. It describes P-Served-User as intended for closed trusted networks, not general Internet use.

sections.title: Why IMS Needs a Served-User Header
sections.content:
The 3GPP IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS) uses SIP for signaling. Its S-CSCF may send a request to an application server, which needs to know whose service profile to use.

Before this header, the served user was inferred from P-Asserted-Identity for originating requests or from the Request-URI for terminating requests. These fields have other meanings and can change during services such as call forwarding, leading an application server to identify the wrong user.
sections.plainLanguage: An application server needs to know which user's preferences and permissions apply to a request. Forwarding can change the address fields it used to make that decision.

sections.title: The Identity Can Outlast a Forwarded Address
sections.content:
The RFC describes cases where a service changes the Request-URI to redirect a call, while later services still need to process the original user's profile. In another case, the call's asserted origin and the user whose profile is being applied are different.

These cases show why the served-user identity and the session case must be conveyed explicitly between the S-CSCF and application server. The RFC says History-Info is not a substitute because it records Request-URI history rather than identifying the served user and session case.
sections.plainLanguage: A redirected call can have a new destination while still being handled for the original user. The header carries that original user's identity directly.

sections.title: The P-Served-User Header
sections.content:
The header contains an identity representing the served user. It may also include sescase, with values orig or term, to indicate an originating or terminating case.

The optional regstate parameter is reg or unreg, indicating whether the user is registered. The header is defined for initial requests for a dialog and standalone requests between nodes in the relevant trust domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The header names the user being served. Optional parameters say whether the request is originating or terminating and whether the user is registered.

sections.title: Proxy Rules for the Header
sections.content:
A supporting proxy must insert P-Served-User only when it can determine the served user and the next hop is in the same trust domain. Otherwise, it must not add the header.

A proxy receiving the header from a trusted node uses its value as the served user. It must remove the header when it came from outside the trust domain or when forwarding to a node outside it.
sections.plainLanguage: Only a proxy that knows the served user may add the header, and only for a trusted next hop. A proxy removes it before the request leaves the trust domain.

sections.title: Trust Domain and Privacy
sections.content:
The served-user value is meaningful only when received securely from a member of the trust domain. The header can reveal user-sensitive information, so proxies must not insert it toward an outside node.

The RFC describes the header as intended for closed trusted networks such as 3GPP IMS, not general Internet use. The trust-domain specification must require member nodes to understand the header.
sections.plainLanguage: The header reveals who a service is acting for, so it must stay among trusted nodes. The RFC limits its intended use to closed networks such as IMS.
